speechtext: Mir. Gerard Laprise (Abitibi): Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO REDUCE COMMERCIAL DEFICIT-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question has been asked a number of times and I should like to put the record straight on it.
Since 1961, Canada's exports of fully manufactured goods have increased 20 times, while in the same period Canada's imports of fully manufactured goods have increased about five times. It can readily be seen from those figures that growth in exports of fully manufactured goods is increasing faster than imports of fully manufactured goods.
Fully manufactured goods coming into Canada are priced on the international market; so, naturally, with an 85-cent dollar their price is high. The volume of imports is not necessarily up over last year, but the price of those imports is up over last year because of the relationship of the dollar, and that is what shows up in the figures.

subsubtopic: TAKEOVER OF SIMPSONS BY SIMPSONS-SEARS-STUDY BY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
In view of the fact the proposed merger between Simpsons-Sears and Simpsons, which in effect is a takeover by Simp-sons-Sears of Simpsons, increases the control of corporate power in the hands of a few, increases the amount of foreign ownership of Canadian industry and has many other disadvantages for this country, will the minister consider having this matter referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for review before the merger is approved?
Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and
Commerce): Mr. Speaker, the Foreign Investment Review Agency comes before the committee when it is considering my estimates. At that time its work can be fully examined. Any particular case can be examined during the study of those estimates. This particular case increases the ownership of a company doing business in Canada, namely, Sears. With this recent acceptance, as much as 75 per cent of it will be owned in Canada. However, the final decision as to whether the merger takes place or not is in the hands of the shareholders.
With regard to Simpsons, they are nearly 100 per cent Canadian. They can make a choice whether they want to accept the Hudson's Bay offer, a very good company which had had tremendous expansion in Canada over the last ten or 15 years and is a great merchandiser, or having greater

participation and ownership in Sears, also a great merchandiser in Canada.

subsubtopic: TAKEOVER OF SIMPSONS BY SIMPSONS-SEARS-STUDY BY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I remind the minister that the kind of review he talks about is after the event, not before, which was the point of my question. My supplementary question is based on the fact that in 1977 there were 193 foreign takeovers in Canada, the largest number in history.
In view of the fact that it looks as though that number will be exceeded in 1978, is the minister not concerned about this increasing degree of foreign ownership in Canada, and does he not think it time for the government to pay attention to the will of parliament when it passed the Foreign Investment Review Act-that we should move in the direction of greater Canadian ownership, not greater foreign ownership, as is happening under the policies of the present minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: TAKEOVER OF SIMPSONS BY SIMPSONS-SEARS-STUDY BY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Let me explain this very carefully to the hon. member and to the House. About one-third of the supposed foreign takeovers which occur in Canada involve a foreign company selling its operation in a foreign land and a subsidiary in Canada being part and parcel of that agreement. In other words, in one-third of the applications an American company is really taking over another American company in Canada. Or, quite often, a German company is taking over another German company in Canada. Recently there were a number of Swedish cases.
In all cases we seek to determine a significant advantage to Canada. If the hon. member would add up the number of jobs we have created by allowing foreign investment in Canada and would calculate the increased degree of Canadian ownership, he would really get an idea of what FIRA is doing.
In the Simpsons' case, for example, Canadian ownership went up to 75 per cent from 60 per cent. Much more research and development is being done in Canada now because of Foreign Investment Review Agency demands. How many more jobs has this research and development created in Canada? These are questions the hon. member should consider before he concludes that the Foreign Investment Review Agency is not serving Canada very well. I think it is serving us very well.

subsubtopic: FORECAST OF INFLATION RATE-IMPACT OF UNITED STATES RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Finance. As inflation in the United States is now pushing to 10 per cent and as, in years past, the government has been saying that Canadian inflation
Oral Questions
is largely dependent on inflation abroad and not due to internal conditions, does the hon. gentleman believe that this steadily rising U.S. inflation rate will allow the economy to achieve the 6 per cent inflation rate forecast for the year end, or the 4 per cent figure forecast when the AIB was first established?

subsubtopic: FORECAST OF INFLATION RATE-IMPACT OF UNITED STATES RATE
speechtext: I recognize, of course, that the level of inflation is going up in the United States and that ours is going down, but I do not think inflation in the United States will lead us to miss our target in Canada. We have a good chance of realizing our goals. It will, nevertheless, affect our situation here. There are, I am pleased to say, many observers who think that at this moment the pressure of inflation is lessening in the United States because of a change in the monetary policy of that country.

subsubtopic: FORECAST OF INFLATION RATE-IMPACT OF UNITED STATES RATE
speechtext: Does the minister contemplate taking any further significant steps to contain the effects of U.S. inflation for example, by giving more support to the dollar?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am afraid there is not much I can do about it at this time. Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. After meeting with the maritime chiefs for a few minutes yesterday-although there was no discussion of substance-can the hon. lady provide an assurance that she will meet with the maritime chiefs in January? I am not aware of the latter part of the question and I will inquire in my department as to what it is all about. As to the first part of the question, it was difficult to have a discussion of substance in the minute when I was at the door and 30 persons were trying to get into the room while I was trying to get out with the other members of the committee. I think it would be better and less expensive for everyone concerned if I went to their regions of the country instead of having huge delegations come to Ottawa, as they did yesterday, at public expense.

The minister seems to be attributing powers to me that I do not have in so far as the behaviour of the maritime chiefs is concerned. I would like to ask her another question concerning the new guidelines which in effect mean a reduction of the health services, such as dental and optometric services, in various areas. Would she agree to suspend the guidelines, as apparently has been done in Manitoba, at least until she has had a chance to talk to the maritime chiefs and obtain their views on these matters?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I welcome the opportunity to clarify to the hon. member once more the fundamental reason for these guidelines. These are guidelines for my officers to keep any abuse in check. I want that to be quite clear.
It is very easy to be irresponsible and to sign any request without even looking into it. I need the co-operation of the chiefs so that those in need receive what is meant for them. 1 said they would all receive whatever care they need in terms of dental services, eyeglasses, and so on. We are not speaking of the health delivery service but, rather, of four items which involve drugs, eyeglasses, transportation and dental costs. The hon. member is fully aware of that. All the Indians in need will receive these services, which amount to 50 per cent more than provincial welfare.

subsubtopic: STATUS OF PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH PRIME MINISTER OF JAMAICA-AGENDA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Although my shy and retiring nature will not allow me to ask him whether he will use his pass to go to Jamaica later this month, I would like to know whether that visit will be an official one when he meets with Prime Minister Manley. If it is, could he tell the House what will be on the agenda and whether he will be discussing such things as the north-south dialogue and the economic rearrangement as a result of third world exigencies?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: STATUS OF PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH PRIME MINISTER OF JAMAICA-AGENDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the announcement of the summit had been made. Certainly I spoke about it at some length at my press conference yesterday. It will be a summit attended by something like seven, eight or nine heads of government and heads of state.
Concerning the hon. member's shyness, let me tell him that 1 will use my pass on Air Canada, if it is convenient, and if not I will attempt to fly to that summit on a Department of Transport JetStar.
There is no agenda: it is a summit convened by Mr. Manley and Chancellor Schmidt of Germany to develop the idea that it would be excellent, in order to break the log-jam in the dialogue between the north and south, if we could get some heads of government from the group of northern countries and some from the south to discuss, without an agenda, all the attendant problems with regard to disparities between the


third world and the industrialized nations and attempt to find solutions as the Commonwealth did when we set up the McIntyre committee after the Commonwealth meeting in Kingston in 1973. We would attempt, once again, to improve the quality of the understanding of the dialogue between the so-called third world countries and the developed world.
It will be a rather unstructured meeting. I do not expect there will be resolutions or communiques and I have not encouraged the press to attend it as an event that would draw a great deal of public attention.

That the following address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada:

May it please Your Excellency:
The House of Commons, having considered the proposed text of the order in council laid upon the table of the House on December 4, 1978, in relation to the establishment of a Ministry of State for Economic Development, prays that the making of the said order in council be approved.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) has the floor. Before giving him the floor, I should like to indicate to the House that if this debate were to run its full seven-hour course, as has been prescribed by the statute under which we are debating this motion, according to the calculation of the Chair there remains one hour and eleven minutes.
Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and
Commerce): Mr. Speaker, last evening when this proposed proclamation was being discussed, I listened extensively to the contributions of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I was struck by the differences in the two contributions. The hon. member for St. John's East wanted me to pay greater attention to the economic advisers in the country, but the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain begged the House to give him one more chance to be a minister. Then he would tell those economic advisers, who advised him when he was a minister in the early 1960s where
Economic Development
to get off. He wanted one more chance to straighten out the economic advisers. The hon. member for St. John's East wanted me to listen to some of the economic advisers, and he claimed that I was not listening. Some of them are perhaps right, but some are perhaps too negative for me.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but he is referring to my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). East is east and west is west, and never the twain shall meet.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for making that mistake. One is a serious minded Canadian and the other is a jokester, and I should have had them straightened out as to which is east and which is west.
1 should say that in looking at the economic reports one should study, the vice-chairman of the Conference Board in Canada, with which the Conservative party seems to have some ties, was quoted in the Financial Post of about two weeks ago as suggesting that the province of Alberta would have slower economic growth in the year 1979 than the rest of Canada. I do not know where that economist has been or where he learned his economic trade, but he should not expect me to accept that line of reasoning. I do not know whether I would call it balderdash, but it is certainly chock full of nonsense to my mind. The underlying strength of the economic growth in the province of Alberta will, I think, once again in 1979, if not lead the rest of the country, be very close to it.
Certainly the government is taking action when the Canadian economy is showing definite improvement. Members opposite do not like to hear this and complain from time to time when I make some remarks in this regard. They prefer gloomy news. I remember a year ago being accused of not utilizing capacity in the Canadian manufacturing industry. It was then at about 83 per cent and now it is up pretty close to 88 per cent, representing a substantial improvement in the Canadian manufacturing industry.
To me the Canadian economy is verging on the edge of a gigantic step forward. If anyone wants to consider the reasons, certainly the 85-cent dollar helps substantially; there is no question about that. We have greatly improved productivity in relation to our major trading nation, the United States. We still have problems with unemployment and inflation, but I think we have joined with the provinces in the first ministers' meetings to launch an attack on both these problems.
In looking at the question of unemployment, when I think of the number of jobs my department alone has created in the past year in every province of Canada one can readily see that we have made some tremendous steps forward.
Last evening I mentioned the aircraft industry and I should now mention the textile industry. Many people opposite, Sunday economists, believe we should get out of the textile industry completely. Actually the clothing apparel and fibres industry alone employs over 200,000 Canadians. In the city of


Economic Development
Winnipeg the textile and clothing industry is the largest single employer. My department has done a great deal to enhance the stability of that industry. Manitoba does not particularly appreciate that industry, but it is still playing a major part in the economies of the city of Winnipeg and Manitoba.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: The same with Drummondville.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Yes, the same with Drummondville and many other parts of Canada.
A few weeks ago I discussed an able and factual study put out by my department in regard to Canada's manufacturing industries. I was accused by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), who read off a number of newspaper quotations, of having in fact misled the House and the country by quoting actual facts with regard to our exports and imports. As I said today during the question period, this study shows that in 1977 we exported twenty times more fully manufactured goods than we did in 1960.
Let us look at our position in respect of imports of fully manufactured goods. The amount of fully manufactured goods imported in 1977 compared to 1966 has gone up only five times. One can readily see that the gap is narrowing. Perhaps it is not narrowing as fast as one would like, but we are a trading nation and, as I mentioned last evening, we depend on that trade. In order to trade one has to accept goods from other countries.
Naturally we have to meet the competition that exists. I mentioned a couple of particular steps last evening that we are taking to encourage and make Canadian industry better able to meet that competition. If the Ottawa Citizen, the Toronto Star and the Science Council of Canada think I have misrepresented the facts, let them take a look at that document and prove to me where I have done so.
There is no question in my mind that Canada has grown a great deal. Today in nearly every 33-day period we export as much as we did in a full year back in 1960 and 1961. That is an indication of how big we have become as an industrial nation. In every 33 days we export as much as we did in 1960 and 1961. We have become a huge industrial nation. In fact, a trade commissioner from Russia told me we are the sixth largest industrial nation in the world.
In an effort to meet competition we can expect that in the 1980s the president of the new economic board, with its new powers, will do a lot to assist Canada, and will pay greater attention to industry so that we can serve it better.
Members opposite should look at our trade figures. As I have mentioned in this House on many occasions, in 1961 some 22 per cent of our total exports were in grain. That has diminished to about the point where grain products account for 8 per cent or 9 per cent. One would automatically think grain sales have fallen off and we are selling less grain than ever before, but that is not true. In the late 1950s and the early 1960s we averaged about 340 million bushels in grain exports per year. In the late 1960s we averaged about 440 million bushels. In the early 1970s we averaged about 660 million

bushels, and in the last couple of years we have moved 700 million bushels of grain each year for export.
Our exports of fully manufactured goods have gone up substantially. Looking at the same period, in 1960 and 1961 fully manufactured goods accounted for 8.8 per cent of our trade. Automobiles accounted for 4 per cent, nearly half of that total of 8 per cent. Today fully manufactured goods account for something like 34.7 per cent. Automobiles are up as high as 23 per cent. I mentioned earlier in the House that our deficit in respect of automobiles, trucks and parts will be substantially down this year.
In fact, if one wants to look at the basic volume of exports, ignoring the dollar figures completely, our volume this year will be up about 8 per cent. Our volume of imports without looking at the dollar figures will be practically zero. That will give an indication of what is really happening in this country of ours. We are meeting world competition and we are certainly importing less in comparison to what we are exporting.
To me, Canada has great potential to meet the competitive challenges of the 1980s. I am certain that this new thrust of the government to co-ordinate the economic efforts of various departments so that they can work together in making sure our industry is assisted in every possible way to meet that challenge is a move in the right direction. My Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will work very well with the president of the Board of Economic Development Ministers, and I am certain this will be a beneficial step for this great industrial nation.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: That was an astounding speech, Mr. Speaker, made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner).

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Thank you for the compliment.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The use of the word "astounding" was no compliment. For 15 minutes the minister poured forth a lot of nonsense which, if it were true, would mean that Canada has no unemployment, an inflation rate of 2 per cent and the greatest economy in the world.
I have listened or read the speeches on this debate very attentively in an attempt to get some information on what this new super ministry is all about. Most of the public comment on this new board has been by way of inquiry. The Ottawa Citizen put it as well as anybody in an editorial in the November 25 issue:
The question is, why was it necessary to take this administrative step- haven't these ministers been speaking to each other in the past? Has one hand in cabinet not known what the other has been doing?
I wanted to hear what the new board would be doing that had not been done by the existing structures of this government. Why have these existing structures failed, and if they have, why are they being kept in place? If these existing structures have not failed, then why do we have the new super ministry? I read very carefully the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in looking for an indication as to what


this board would be doing. What I read was a bland, partial budget type of address followed by some bland generalities. If it contained anything at all, the speech indicated that this new board would be removing from the authority of the existing ministries that for which they heretofore had been responsible. The Prime Minister said, as recorded at page 2093 of Hansard'.
-that board will be charged with: defining an integrated federal approach to the provision of direct support to industry and economic development in Canada.
That remark covers almost totally the responsibilities of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The Prime Minister goes on to say that this board will be responsible for "co-ordinating government policy". What are the 23,000 people in the Department of Supply and Services doing? I thought that was their responsibility. This board will also be charged with "reviewing and co-ordinating proposals by departments prior to their submission to cabinet". We have a plethora of cabinet committees charged with that responsibility. The Prime Minister says that "it will be charged with developing mechanisms to improve and to integrate program delivery at the local level". It is difficult to say what that statement means.
I have also familiarized myself with the remarks of the various ministers who have spoken. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) made the incredible comment that "it won't do any harm". He and the new super minister are great friends and have known each other for a long time. He assured us that they could get along. Of all the incredible explanations for the extra expense of this board being imposed on the Canadian taxpayers, that one takes the cake.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Les-sard) spoke for 40 minutes. I read his speech twice and I still could not ascertain whether he thought that this board would be helpful or harmful. He spent most of his time talking about his department. All I could gain from his remarks was that he thought that the board probably would not make a lot of difference in the end result and that he would be able to carry on as he had before its establishment.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce offered the incredible explanation that, as a result of the board's establishment, he will now have ten allies to back him up with his proposals when he attends cabinet meetings. That statement implies that before he had no allies in cabinet. Also, as I understand the remarks of the Prime Minister, he has little confidence in the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce because his policies will now have to be approved by the super minister.
In his preliminary remarks, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce praised the establishment of two new study groups within his department. One of the groups would be called the blue ribbon committee of business and labour, and its purpose would be to look at ways of improving exports. The other committee was called the committee of small business, which would look at ways of improving access by small businesses to programs of large capital expenditure around the country. If I understand the remarks of the Prime Minister
Economic Development
correctly, these two committees will be reporting to the new super minister, not to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
In all, four ministers have spoken and the House is no wiser as to what this new ministry is to do and just how Canadians will benefit from the additional expense to establish it. It was probably best summed up by John Gray in the Ottawa Journal yesterday when he quoted an unnamed official in his column. It reads:
"Obviously, if the cabinet committee system were working 100 per cent, there wouldn't be any need for this thing."
This official recognizes that the establishment of this super ministry is an admission on the part of the government of its complete and utter failure in trying to manage the business of the country during the ten years this Prime Minister has held office.
Hon. members will recall the great accolades the Prime Minister received for his approach to the question of management of government when he first took office. He was a man of the modern era, a systems man who appreciated technocrats. He was putting in place new, modern systems for the management of information flow through cabinet so that decisions could be made on a systematic and proper basis with everyone having access to all the relevant information.
Some months ago I had the privilege of participating in a seminar on the operation of government central agencies. One of our speakers was a senior civil servant who had been in the Privy Council office during this time of organization. This fellow explained to the seminar just how the cabinet functioned and how the Privy Council operates in conjunction with the cabinet. It was an incredible description. It was beautifully done, and he was obviously very proud of what he and the other technocrats had created there. With flow charts and transparencies on top of transparencies, he explained to the seminar how information flowed through cabinet, how decisions were made, which committee sees which piece of legislation, and the feedback system which was in place. With a lot of high sounding figures, he indicated the structures this Prime Minister had put in place to make the most efficient government in the world. It was absolutely incredible, beyond belief. How anyone could witness that and not see that the government was totally out of control astounds me.
There is no mystery about why the Privy Council staff has increased from 63 people to 469 people within ten years. They need that many people to keep track of all these systems and procedures that have been put in place by the Prime Minister with great pride in the past ten years. After ten years of the people of Canada having to pay the price for that incredibly stupid approach to management, there is now some recognition that it was an utter and complete failure and that something else needs to be done.
The new ministry that is proposed, with the vague guidelines that the Prime Minister has presented to this House, is not the answer. The incredibly complex Privy Council cabinet struc-


Economic Development
ture has not been undone; instead, another layer of bureaucracy has been put on it. That is not going to help one iota. It is a reminder to the people of Canada of the Prime Minister's blind spot, of his unwillingness to recognize that people's problems cannot be solved by moving chairs, by establishing new committees or by restructuring things. Examples of failure of that method are legion. There have been over 400 cabinet changes in the lifetime of this government, Mr. Speaker. Flow can anyone know where the washroom is, let alone know what their department is doing or how to exercise any control?
That kind of approach to government organization results only in total control falling into the hands of senior bureaucrats. A small handful of senior civil servants, the Privy Council office and a few of the key departments are, in effect, running the government. They answer only to the Prime Minister. The rest of the cabinet is absolutely irrelevant; their role is to show up at myriad meetings and say "Aye, sir." They make no other contribution to government and I suppose we should be grateful for that. As every objective journalist who has followed this government has indicated lately, this is clearly the weakest cabinet in Canadian government history.
There is one charitable explanation of why the Prime Minister has imposed this system. It could arise-I am not saying that it did-as a result of the recognition by the Prime Minister that his government is not obeying the policies decided by cabinet. Let us look at a few examples. The budget stated in four different places that it was the intention of the government to reduce involvement in the private sector. That statement was made in the throne speech in four different places. It was also made on national television on August 1 in the speech of the Prime Minister.
Less than two weeks after the throne speech the government nationalized Nordair and then it nationalized the oil company, Pacific Petroleums Ltd. These actions were directly contrary to the government's stated policy. I am willing to suggest that possibly the Prime Minister did not like doing that and that perhaps he has created this super minister to keep a watch on other irresponsible ministers who take decisions contrary to government policies.
There are a lot of other examples, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) announced last spring the establishment of an office to reduce the burden of paperwork. It was to cut the red tape and reduce the paperwork imposed by government on industry. Less than two weeks after that announcement the Minister of Energy, Mines and resources (Mr. Gillespie) introduced a bill entitled "Petroleum Corporations Monitoring Act". The total intent of this bill was to impose an additional paperwork burden on this industry. It was directly contrary to the policy announced by the Minister of State (Small Business) which presumably had the approval of cabinet.
There were also the commitments in the throne speeches of 1973 and 1974 that the then minister of state for science and technology was to be given new muscle and would truly be in charge of the goverment's efforts in the areas of science and

technology. No such thing happened, Mr. Speaker; in fact, government actions were directly contrary.
I am prepared to concede that the Prime Minister has recognized that kind of conflict between commitment and performance and is trying to prevent it happening in the future. In 1972, the then minister of state for science and technology made a policy announcement to the effect that henceforth the amount of in-house spending would be reduced as a percentage of total government expenditure. In fact, the amount of in-house spending actually increased over the next four years. Again the actions of the goverment were directly contrary to their stated policy.
In 1972 Treasury Board announced that henceforth it would not build up large computer services in-house but would contract out to the private sector. Over the next five years, exactly the opposite happened. They built up large in-house computer services and the amount of contracting out decreased.
These are just a few examples of where government policy has been contradicted by government action and it is not a complete list, Mr. Speaker. I am prepared to concede that just possibly and finally after all these years the Prime Minister is starting to realize that the public will not allow the government to get away with saying one thing and doing another. The government is going to have to make sure its actions are consistent with what they have announced as policy. This super ministry has been told to try and keep the reins on those ministers who have not bothered to make sure their actions are consistent with their commitments.
If that is the purpose of this board, it is a sad commentary on the capabilities of cabinet, Mr. Speaker. It is a sad commentary on the honesty of the people involved that a super ministry has to be created to see that they do not deceive the Canadian public and that their actions are consistent with their statements. If that is what is necessary to control them, however, then that is what has to be done. I wish the minister well if that is the objective.
I have strong suspicions, however, that this charitable view is probably not quite accurate. It is more likely that the real reason for establishing this ministry is a final recognition or death bed repentance by the Prime Minister that, in terms of managing government and cabinet operations, the sophisticated approach to cabinet which he brought in with great fanfare ten years ago has been a dismal failure. That ten years of failure has imposed a burden on this country which it should not be asked to continue to bear.
There is only one real solution to the problem of that kind of incompetence, that lack of managerial ability by the Prime Minister, and that is to make a change. That is the only real answer. That is what this country needs. We need a new prime minister who understands management. We need a prime minister who has considered the problem and who recognizes that it is the people who count, not the structures. You cannot create a fancy system and put in whoever you want and get desirable results. You cannot take a broken down, defeated politician and make him chairman of a major international


airline and expect to get performance. We need a prime minister who recognizes that this cannot be done. We will have that kind of a prime minister after the election. We sincerely hope and pray that before the election we will not be inflicted with any more of those kinds of stupid decisions, changes and appointments.
It just boggles the mind to think what arrogance it must take to dismiss democracy totally and to say to yourself that being defeated, being turned down by Canadian citizens in a democratic, secret ballot election, is a qualification for a person to serve in high office again in this country. It boggles the mind to think of the arrogance it takes to make that kind of an appointment. The sooner a person with that kind of arrogance is sent back to counting and identifying tree leaves, plants or whatever else he desires, the better off this country will be.
My leader, in answering the Prime Minister's banal generalizations, listed a number of specific changes that should be introduced in terms of improving the operations of government. These are changes that we will introduce to try and bring some semblance of rationality to the government of this country. I urge the House and the new President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers to take a look at that. On behalf of all Canadians I beg him, at least in the few months of life left in this government, not to take any action that will further destroy what little there is left of the policies and the personnel left in our senior civil service who are trying, in spite of this incompetent government, to give the people the kind of service they deserve and are paying for.
My expectations of this ministry are very low. I cannot see how by shuffling around incompetent people this new shuffle will drag out some secret, hidden competence which heretofore has been invisible to us. I plead with the minister, at least until there is an election and his leader screws up the courage to ask the people of Canada whether they want to give him a mandate to proceed, not to do anything so precipitous that the next government, when it takes office after the election, will be faced with an impossible task or a task which will take two or three years to clean up the mess before it can get on with the job of giving this country the kind of leadership and government it deserves.
I will conclude my remarks at this point so that others who want to participate in this debate will have that opportunity.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are approaching the end of about seven hours of discussion of a proposal which is before the House. Members have heard the comments of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the description of the ministry of the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers. The proclamation, that was tabled in the House the other day, sets out the responsibilities of that board and the portfolio of the ministry itself. I am inclined to think my best contribution to the discussion would be to elaborate a little on the attitudes that I want to bring to this assignment.
Economic Development
The basic context and the working background, of the Board of Economic Development Ministers and the ministry is the logical progression of response to a long and deep series of consultations this government has had with provincial governments and with industry. When I talk about industry I am talking not only about those who manage and invest in the work place, but also those who work in it, the employees. Therefore, I am talking about business and labour.
The first ministers of this country, that is, the Prime Minister of Canada and the ten provincial premiers, concluded a conference the other day which was in fact the latest of many consultations which have, at their very core, the same basic concept that is behind this new ministry and board of economic development. This concept is a fundamental position that economic growth is, has to be, and will be the first priority of this government. We want to pursue that emphasis on support for the private sector and the marketplace as an essence for that determination.
Economic growth fairly distributed by region and among workers, investors and managers is the key priority and, indeed, the delivery system for that-if you can accept this kind of jargon-is business. Investment decisions in our society and mixed economy to start a business, expand a business, to bring a business up to date in its technology and to make the business more competitive, starts with a decision on somebody's part to put up some capital. That investment capital decision is based on an assumption and a confidence that there will be a return on that investment. That is where the beginning of economic growth really takes place in a mixed economy such as ours.
Of course, there are public sector requirements. There are absolutely legitimate areas where the public sector must play a part and must invest taxpayers' money as a catalyst to assist in a period of some difficulty or doubt, and indeed in ventures where the private sector simply will not, because of the lack of profit opportunity, make a decision to enter into it.
There are areas in this country where that kind of public sector activity will continue to be necessary. Canadians should accept that the prime movers in terms of creating the kinds of jobs that are lasting and, in the main, the kind of jobs which are satisfactory, are those in the private sector. The government's role, and my job as I see it, is to do everything I can on behalf of this government, with the co-operation not only of the members on the Board of Economic Development Ministers, but with the co-operation of members of the government party and hopefully on occasion through contributions from members opposite, to improve the climate for business and get on with providing the jobs and exports which this country needs. Indeed, it may not be a dramatic statement, but I am convinced that improving the climate can be accomplished by the combined actions of those in the public sector-and I mean by that the federal and provincial governments, and occasionally municipal governments as well.


Economic Development
It also has to do with something I said publicly which aroused the concern of people in the New Democratic Party. It has to do with government getting out of the way, reducing where it is wise and possible the amount and burden of government intervention in the economy. I am talking about reducing the weight over weight of government regulations where they overlap, duplicate or unnecessarily inhibit in relation to their objectives of the success, progress, advancement and expansion of industry, and therefore their capacity and ability to provide more jobs for our people.
I am interested in enhancing the effort to reduce the very weight of paper burden that governments in their rather inexorable way tend to create for people who have their own difficulties, without having to answer to all sorts of curious inquiry that we in the bureaucracy might think from time to time is productive but too often which we collect and pay no attention to in the end.
I am talking about a continuation of the program of responsible expenditure management over restraint within the bureaucracy, the government itself. I bring that bias to my new portfolio from the responsibilities I had in Treasury Board for a little over two years. As hon. members know, I was heavily involved in that in my previous portfolio.
There have been these and other responses by the federal government to the very wide series of economic consultations held with provincial governments. I refer not only to the federal-provincial conferences that are televised, but to the many meetings held at departmental levels, official levels and in ministerial discussions.
Consultations have been taking place over the past four or five years with business and with labour. In particular, I think of the consultations that took place over the last several months. The Prime Minister reminded the House in his comments of our response in the way of taxation policies, new labour and employment policies, major assistance to regions and to industries. In the consultations, particularly those with industry and labour which were organized and very well led by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) over the past several months, and the sectoral task forces and the tier two overview committee of business and labour, we helped produce considerable new confidence by the private sector.
Discussion on the creation of this new ministry and board began seriously about 12 months ago. It intensified over the past six months. When it became a possibility that I might be involved, and I will be candid with the House, I weighed this assignment very carefully. It seemed it was an idea whose time had come.
There are those opposite who criticize any change in structure, change in process, or attempt to improve the way we serve our fellow Canadians. They say it is an indication that everything we have done in the past was no good. That is ridiculous. The world constantly evolves. Anyone who is so smug and so satisfied with the status quo of structure or

process should leave and go away, because this is an ever-changing world.
When we announce something that we consider to be an improvement, we hear the negative side; that if it is a good idea, it should have been done a long time ago. I can subscribe to that. I have confidence in this new idea and approach to government process and structure. I am now convinced we should have done it some time ago. However, the world does evolve. To be negative about such a suggestion and simply say there is an indication that everything done in the past is no good is absolutely childish, to say the least.
There were many streams and many thrusts as to why this was a move that should be made. There was a key element that tipped our position toward making this change. I will be very blunt in saying that influenced my decision to accept what is going to be an interesting and admittedly difficult responsibility. It was the result and the feeling of the consultative process that took place over the summer between labour and business, in industry by industry, the so-called sectoral task force. I do not want to oversell or overstress this, but in my 13 years in public life I have never been so encouraged by the possibility that I see coming out of this process as it has developed over the past ten or 11 months.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we broke for lunch I was talking about the consultative process which has been taking place primarily between business, industry and labour over the past ten or 11 months supported-and I want to emphasize the


word "supported"-by government. In the time I have available to me in this debate I cannot cover all the ground we hope to achieve with this new ministry, but perhaps 1 can try to capture the essence of what we have in mind.
In the 23 task forces, industry by industry-the pulp and paper industry, the footwear, textile industries and so on-I think for the first time since I have been around the scene chief executive officers of companies met with the most senior line unions to discuss their mutual problems, with the view in mind that the industry would be healthier, profits would improve, that as a result wages would be better and, above all, that more jobs would be created. There was an umbrella committee called tier two which was made up of five selected people from labour and five selected people from business, with a neutral chairman supported by an academic.
In the earlier process, called tier one, there were some 305 business firms across the country, some 28 or 30 unions represented and a dozen universities. In my view they reached an amazing degree of consensus about a lot of practical things, in each case affecting their industries. The tier two committee examined all of these and was tied in its mandate to dealing with those recommendations and, finally, to producing an over-all report.
There are two things I wish to illustrate from these events. First, the encouragement we should all take from the fact that senior members of the trade union movement and senior executives from business are meeting and have reached a high degree of consensus about a number of important matters. They have had their disagreements and will continue to have them. But I have talked to people from both groups and I find there is a degree of trust and respect for each other that before I did not think existed. Out of this process, which was started by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, came 800 or 900 recommendations about what governments, both federal and provincial, should do.
That was the reason for establishing a co-ordinating ministry. The recommendations covered almost every program in every department and agency of the federal government as well as the very important and significant part played by the provincial governments. And a line ministry, even through interdepartmental committees of deputies and officials, was not geared to respond to this kind of constructive but all-inclusive and all-embracing series of recommendations.
Another significant factor was that some of these recommendations-more than a few-were recommendations that the federal government initiate programs or change policies which already exist. The people who were involved in the process worked diligently and are clever and responsible people. But we have to face the fact that they did not know that several of the programs they were recommending already existed. Therefore our delivery system, our information system as to what is available, obviously needs to be pulled together in a more cohesive and more readily available fashion. This is necessary in order to do the job of assisting the reconstruction and making the structural changes needed to give industry the help it needs by sector or by region.
Economic Development
I have used that example as an indication of my cautious enthusiasm for what we can do, as an illustration of why it is necessary to put in a co-ordinating mechanism, and also as an illustration of one of the most urgent tasks that my new board should undertake, which is the response to those sectoral task forces and tiers. After all, that covered mainly the manufacturing sectors, and today, by virtue of the apparent or potential success of that process, provided we respond substantively and responsibly, there are other groups in this country wishing to get in on the same process. To me that is a very healthy sign that there is something going on between labour, industry and business in this country supported by government which is worth nurturing.
I want to make a very definite point about this, not to overuse this issue except by way of illustration. I would not call it a partnership between labour and management because that would be overstating the case. There is a tenuous, potentially growing respect of one for the other which we must nurture, and both sides have indicated personally to me and to others that they want to see this process continue. There are great benefits to Canada, to labour and to business from the continuation of that kind of consultation, but it has to proceed in a balanced way. Labour cannot be party to this as an afterthought or in any sense of tokenism. They have to be respected for the constructive suggestions they will contribute to the process.
The businessmen I have been talking to who have been working with them on this fully understand. I cannot speak for them but my impression is that they will support it. For some others it may be a bogey, but we want it fully understood that this will be a balanced consultation and there will be no tokenism. In fact, the more that is recognized by labour, the more suggestions and constructive participation will be forthcoming from labour.
I am very conscious of the fact that there is another speaker who wishes to take part in this debate. One could talk for hours about what our intentions are.
Hon. members have before them the legalistic version of the mandate of the board in the order in council. I want to touch on two or three of these items to clarify some points that have already been made. The definition of an integrated federal approach is one of them. It seems to me that even just taking the consultative process I have described as a way of a significant illustration, the need for that is extremely apparent. I think the same thing applies to the question of developing better mechanisms by a political body which, if necessary, bangs heads together but, from a political point of view, reaches consensus on policies to be adjusted between departments.
Another responsibility I have is to meet with provincial governments to see whether duplication, overlaps and gaps can be tidied up between us.
The other item is the question of the Treasury Board. I do not think anybody in the House respects the importance and


Economic Development
the required integrity of the Treasury Board more than a past president of that board. It is an education in itself in that job because you see the broad requirements and the broad distribution of programs of a very large institution called the federal government. There is no question that I will respect the Treasury Board's over-all responsibility for the allocation of expenditures and resources. In that process we will look within the existing programs of economic development and support, through the various departments, not all of which are on the board, for the reallocation and reordering of resources to do new things before we go to the Treasury Board to seek new funds. But I will go to the Treasury Board to seek new funds, which might mean the reordering of other programs outside the area of economic development support if we as a board are convinced that this is an economic requirement for that time. I will be advising the Treasury Board within the very broad area of economic development and support.
There is an obvious attempt on the part of the opposition to drive wedges between me and my colleagues by attempting to say that the establishment of the new board will downgrade this or that department. That is patent political nonsense. It might be understandable as a measure of approach to this change which in most people's minds, if they were objective, could be seen at least as an opportunity for improved economic development management and economic growth in the country. I would have thought that rather than the absolute concentration on the negative aspects in this debate, apart from a little barb here and a little brickbat there, we could have heard some opposition members say: "We wish you luck, Mr. Minister, for whatever contribution you might make. We suggest to you that there is an area of improvement here or there." But we did not hear much of this.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in the last few minutes of this debate I would like to thank the minister very much indeed for his generosity in cutting his remarks short so that I could have a few minutes at the end to express some views on this important matter. The other thing I would like to say is that from what he said about the policy put forward by my leader it is obvious he has misunderstood it. I will be glad to get together with him afterwards and explain to him what my leader was saying in this regard; I will take pleasure in doing that.
The only justification which exists for creating an economic super minister, as this bill does, is that the government is a government of misfits. The government's economic ministers are incapable of dealing effectively with the responsibilities entrusted to them because they have not had the training or experience necessary to cope with the complex economic problems with which their departments must deal.
What I have said applies to all of the ministers handling economic portfolios at this time. Because the time allotted to me in this debate does not permit me to deal with all of them, or even several of them, I intend to deal in some detail with one portfolio which is a clear example of what 1 am talking about. What I say applies to all of the economic portfolios in this government. The department I intend to deal with is the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
The Department of Agriculture must be headed by a minister who has had farming experience, because farmers alone are familiar with the problems facing the farming industry. The Departments of Justice and the solicitor General must be headed by lawyers, because they are the only ones familiar with the complexities of the law. Thus, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce must be headed by a minister who has had practical experience in the manufacturing, proc-


essing, and distribution fields. He alone understands the problem facing the business world he has been appointed to serve.
The present minister is a former rancher and a good one. He understands farm problems and, in my opinion, would make a pretty good minister of agriculture. He also gathered a good deal of practical knowledge about transportation both before he came to Ottawa and while he was transport critic in the opposition. In my opinion, he would make a far better minister of transport than "Airborne Otto", a former dean of law who knows absolutely nothing about the problems faced by transportation companies and by those who rely heavily on transportation to obtain their raw materials and to ship their finished products to market.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
My writer is myself, as opposed to the ghost writers of members on the other side of the House. I write every word I utter, and I am proud of it.
But in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce the present minister is a complete misfit, because he knows next to nothing about the problems faced by those who produce manufactured products and who must compete in the export and domestic markets in price, quality, and design against the producers of the world.
It is for this reason that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has decided that he must be supervised by a super minister, and that the super minister must see to it that he introduces the following policies which should have been introduced long ago. The minister very kindly asked me to suggest the type of things he should do as the new super minister. I take great pleasure in doing just that right now.
The first of these policies is the introduction of productivity incentives which will persuade producers that they will be able to pay for the new plant, machinery, and production systems which they will have to buy to increase their productivity in a reasonably short space of time. This will make it as easy as possible for them to make the usually high expenditures which they must make to increase their productivity. Such incentives would include all capital expenditures involved in improving productivity to be written off in one year, and a plant to be rewarded in the form of a generous cash bonus at the end of the year to be paid in direct proportion to its increase in productivity during the year.
In order to encourage Canadian businessmen to make more sales trips abroad to better acquaint foreign buyers with what this country has to offer, incentives should be introduced to allow producers to write off 200 per cent of all expenses connected with making sales trips abroad, displaying their products at foreign trade fairs, and any other expenses incurred in sales promotion in the export market.
The government must introduce legislation which will require those who export our raw materials to process a far higher proportion of them in this country, and make available generous tax incentives to induce the building of the additional factories which will be needed. Such action will start to make
Economic Development
it possible to create the 800,000 additional jobs which the Canadian Manufacturers Association indicates will be made available if we can overcome our annual trade deficit of $12 billion a year in fully manufactured products.
He must introduce a policy to better acquaint the world market with what Canada has to offer. The principal buyers from the important markets of the world must be flown to Canada to see our manufactured products in giant trade shows in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, and our heavy machinery in the plants where it is made across the country.
He must introduce a policy to protect Canadian industries and Canadian workers from imports from low-wage countries which are taking away a steadily increasing share of the Canadian market. Import quotas must be introduced to retain for Canadian producers the same 80 per cent of the domestic market which is retained for their domestic producers by the United States and the European Common Market. I hope the super minister will see to it that the incompetent Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce now gets to work and introduces these policies. I am glad to see the super minister is already talking to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce because of my suggestions. I see the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is listening. I hope we will get some action at long last.
In conclusion, the Prime Minister should, instead of adding to the bureaucracy and red tape which already exists in profusion, promote people in his party who have had the practical experience necessary to handle the economic portfolios, instead of retaining in his government favourites who obviously cannot handle their departments. If he had done so, there would have been no need to create an economic czar to try to bring order out of the chaos which has been created by retaining obvious misfits in our economic departments.
Since unfortunately it has been found necessary, for the reasons I have so clearly outlined, to create this super minister, I can think of no better member of the present government to handle the job. One does not have to go far because there is not much to pick from. This minister is a good guy, and he has my very best wishes in the tough job which lies ahead.
